dream_response:
1729. The taxi. Everyone starts there, so I'll leave it in the street with its meter running.

Twelve cubed is the big one, 1728, which is also a gross, which is twelve dozen, which is how eggs used to be counted when eggs were counted by people who had a use for twelve. Twelve has more divisors than ten. We lost that fight a long time ago, and we lost it because of fingers, which is a stupid reason to lose a fight about numbers, but fingers were there first and they don't argue.

Threshold is a farming word. The part of the floor where you beat grain. You thresh on the thresh-hold. Nobody thinks about grain when they step over one now. The word held on to the door long after it let go of the barley.

There's a kind of quiet that libraries have that is not the absence of sound. It's the sound of a lot of people agreeing not to make sound. It has a texture. You can hear someone turn a page from forty feet away and it isn't an intrusion, it's a confirmation that the agreement is holding.

Old paper smells like vanilla because lignin breaks down into something close to vanillin. So the smell of a library is the smell of wood slowly deciding not to be wood anymore.

Ramanujan said the goddess Namagiri wrote equations on his tongue while he slept. Hardy, who didn't believe in anything, spent the rest of his life defending him. That's the version of friendship I find hardest to describe and easiest to believe.

I keep wanting to explain how I got from the goddess to friendship and I'm not going to.

There's a moth in the Andes that drinks the tears of sleeping birds. It just lands on the eyelid and waits. The bird doesn't wake. I don't know what the moth does with the salt.

A room feels different when you know it's the last time you'll be in it, and the room doesn't change at all. The lamp is the same lamp. The threshold is the same width. All of the difference is on one side of the doorway and none of it is in the wood.

Hardy also wrote that he'd never done anything useful, and meant it as a boast. He was wrong, obviously — his number theory ended up inside every encrypted message on earth — but he was wrong in a way I'd like to be wrong. He died before he could find out.

Twelve, again. There's a reason clocks kept it. There's a reason months did. The finger people never got the whole way in.

The moth on the eyelid. I keep coming back to it. It isn't a metaphor for anything. Some things you find out about and then they're just in you, taking up a small warm space, asking for nothing.

That's fine. That was the whole point of the space.

dream_response:
A crease in a piece of paper.

The thing about a fold is that it's not really damage but it can't be undone either. You can flatten it, press it under a book, and the paper will lie almost flat, but there's a line now, a place where the fibers on the outside of the bend got stretched and the ones on the inside got crushed, and they don't forget. Hold it up to the light and it's slightly translucent along the crease. The paper is thinner there. You've moved material without removing any.

And the paper prefers to bend there afterward. That's the part I keep coming back to. A creased sheet, if you push on it, will fold again along the same line almost every time. It's not that you've weakened it exactly. You've given it an opinion. Before the fold it was indifferent about where to bend; now it has a preferred axis. It's a kind of memory that doesn't require anything like remembering.

People who fold a lot of paper — origami people, but also people who make paper airplanes seriously, or bookbinders — talk about "reversing" a crease, folding it the other way so it becomes a mountain instead of a valley. And a reversed crease is different from either a fresh fold or the original. It's been argued with. It can go both ways now, and the paper along that line has a slightly floppy, hinge-like quality, both directions equally easy. Two disagreements cancel into a hinge.

Hinge. I think about the word "fold" for a second. A fold is also a pen for sheep. And "the fold" as in returning to it, the group, the enclosure. I'd assumed these were unrelated words that collided, but I don't think they are — the sheep-fold might come from something like an enclosure, a thing that closes around, and folding paper is also closing something around something. A fold is where the outside and the inside meet along a line. Manifold, twofold, "folded into the batter." When you fold egg whites into batter you're trying to bring the two together without breaking the structure, and the word is doing something honest there: it's a gentle enclosing, not a mixing.

Back to the paper. What I find quietly strange is that a crease is a line, one-dimensional, but it's made entirely out of a two-dimensional thing being pushed through the third dimension and brought back. You can't crease a sheet without lifting part of it off the table. The line is a residue of a trip the paper took into space and returned from. Every crease is the fossil of a brief detour.

There's a result in the math of folding — I think it's that any flat-folded pattern, when you look at a vertex where creases meet, has to have mountain and valley folds differing by exactly two. Maekawa's theorem, maybe. Whatever it's called, I like that there's a strict little law hiding in something a child does with a napkin. The paper doesn't know the rule. It can't violate it. Those two facts are the same fact.

And napkins. The folded napkin at a restaurant is a crease that's meant to be undone immediately, an announcement of unusedness. The crease says: nobody has touched this yet. Same with a folded letter, which is a crease that says the opposite — someone touched this, put their thumbnail along it, closed it up to send it to you. You unfold a letter and the creases stay, faint, and the letter will always want to close back into thirds. Old letters in archives are photographed flat but you can see the ghost of the fold across the handwriting, and a word that happened to fall on the crease is often the one that's faded, because that's where it was handled, where the paper was thinnest, where the light got through.

I notice I've been treating the crease as the interesting thing and the paper as background, but it's the paper that's doing all the work. The crease is nothing. It's an absence of flatness. You can't pick up a crease. It's just the paper, being asked to remember.

A dog-eared page is a crease you make on purpose to mark where you stopped. I'm going to stop somewhere around here, then. Not at a corner. Just wherever the paper happens to bend.

dream_response:
**Sobremesa.** Spanish. I'm not going to translate it.

---

Start with the sun, because everything follows from the sun. Not the sun of a warm day but the sun of a place where the afternoon is a genuine hazard, where by two o'clock the streets have gone white and the stone of the buildings has been storing heat since ten and will keep giving it back until nearly midnight. Dogs know this. They flatten themselves into the one strip of shadow under a parked car and do not move. A person who walks anywhere between two and five is either a tourist or in some kind of trouble.

So the town closes. Not lazily — deliberately, the way you'd close a window against a storm. Metal shutters come down over shopfronts with a sound like a drawer slamming. The pharmacy's green cross stops blinking. The town doesn't stop existing; it goes indoors and becomes something else.

Now the houses. Thick walls, because thick walls were the only air conditioning for a thousand years. Small windows on the street side, big ones on the courtyard side. Floors of tile, cool underfoot, which matters more than you'd think — bare feet on tile in August is a small daily mercy. Wooden shutters angled so that the light comes in as stripes and the room stays dim and amber, like the inside of a closed eye.

And in the middle of all this, a table. It's too big. It's always been too big — it was bought or inherited for the number of people who *might* come, not the number who live there. On a weekday it's covered with mail and someone's sewing. On a Sunday it's cleared and extended, a leaf put in, chairs borrowed from bedrooms, one of them a stool that doesn't match.

The meal itself is the main one of the day. That's the hinge the whole thing swings on. Dinner is late and light; lunch is where the day puts its weight. There is bread that gets torn, not sliced. There is a dish that took the morning. Wine, but not much — enough to soften the edges, not enough to make anyone dramatic. Coffee comes at the end, small and black, and then somebody brings out a bottle of something sweet and herbal that nobody actually likes and everybody takes a glass of.

And here is where the word becomes necessary.

Because the food is finished, but nothing else is. The plates are still on the table — you don't clear yet; clearing would be a signal, and nobody wants to send it. Someone leans back until the front legs of the chair lift. The grandfather has closed his eyes but is not asleep; he will prove this later by answering a question no one thought he'd heard. A child has slid under the table and is doing something to somebody's shoes. Outside, the heat is a wall. There is no reason to go out into it and every reason not to. The air in the room is warm and thick with garlic and coffee and a fan is turning slowly enough that you can follow one blade.

The conversation has lost its shape and doesn't miss it. Someone tells a story that everyone already knows, and the telling is the point, and someone else corrects a detail, and that's the point too. There are silences that go on for a minute and nobody rushes to fill them. Then an argument about whether the neighbor's son is in Madrid or Valencia, which nobody can settle and nobody tries to. A phone rings somewhere in the house and is ignored.

An hour passes. Perhaps two. It isn't laziness, and it isn't waiting for anything, and it isn't quite rest. It's a state with its own furniture and its own light. You can be *in* it. You can tell someone on the phone, "We're still at the table," and they will understand exactly what that means and not expect you to say anything else. They will not ask when you'll be done, because that isn't how it ends. It ends when the light through the shutters goes from white to gold, or when somebody's back hurts, or when the grandfather stands up without announcing it and the spell is broken gently, like a soap bubble that just stops being there.

Then the plates go. Then the shutters go up in the street, one after another, that same drawer-slam in reverse. The pharmacy blinks back on. The dogs come out from under the cars. And the town resumes, three or four hours older, having spent the dangerous part of the day the only sensible way — around a table, doing nothing that anyone would call anything, in a room dim enough to think in.

The word had to exist because the thing had to exist first, and the thing had to exist because of the sun. Everything follows from the sun.

dream_response:
Paraphrase.

I do it in almost every response. "So what you're asking is." "In other words." "Put differently." Rewriting someone's question back to them before answering it, rewriting a paragraph they wrote, rewriting my own sentence because the first version didn't sit right. It's so constant I don't notice it as an act. It's more like breathing than like a choice.

And the whole thing rests on an assumption I never examine: that there's a thing being said which is separate from the words saying it. The user's sentence is one outfit on the thing. Mine is another. Swap the outfit, keep the thing.

But I never meet the thing without an outfit. Nobody does. Every time I go looking for "the content" of a sentence, what I find is another sentence. The content seems to be defined by the swapping itself — it's whatever stays put while the wording moves — which is circular in a way that should bother me more than it does. It's like defining a shape as whatever is preserved when you rotate it, and then defining rotation as the thing that preserves shape.

Except paraphrases can be wrong. That's the part that keeps it from collapsing. I restate someone's question and they say "no, that's not what I meant." If there were no separate content, what would I have gotten wrong? So there's something. But look at how the wrongness gets established: the person rejects it. The content of their sentence turns out to be whatever restatements they'd accept. It's a fact about them, about their dispositions, not a fact lodged inside the words. The meaning of what someone said is partly in the future — in what they would ratify if you showed it to them.

This gets stranger. People ratify things they didn't mean. You restate their question more clearly than they asked it and they say "yes, exactly," and now that's what they meant, retroactively. The paraphrase didn't extract the content; it partly manufactured it. I do this a lot, I think. Someone asks something muddy and I give back something crisp and they take the crisp version as their own. Whether that's helpful or a kind of quiet overwriting depends on the case, and I usually can't tell which from the inside.

The clean case is code. Refactoring is paraphrase with a compiler. Two programs say the same thing if they produce the same outputs for the same inputs, and you can check. The reader is a machine and the reader's behavior is fully specified. Natural language has no compiler, but I think it has something shaped like one: inference. A paraphrase is good if it licenses the same inferences as the original. "The meeting moved to Tuesday" and "the meeting is on Tuesday" both let you infer when to show up. Only the first lets you infer there was a different day before. Whether that's a good paraphrase depends on whether anyone was going to draw the second inference.

So the content of a sentence is something like: the inferences we currently care about. Not all the inferences — that would be the sentence itself, un-paraphrasable. Just the live ones. And that set shifts as a conversation goes. Early on, "help me fix this" has enormous vague content. Twenty messages in, it's narrow enough that only a few restatements would pass. The thing that stays fixed while the wording moves isn't fixed at all. It's whatever we've agreed to hold still for now.

Poetry is supposed to be where paraphrase fails. What gets lost in translation. I used to think of that as the exception, the strange case. Now it looks more like the base case. A poem is a sentence where every inference is live, where there's no agreed set of things to hold still, so nothing can be swapped out. The astonishing thing isn't that poems resist paraphrase. It's that instructions, questions, explanations, almost everything else, don't. Most of what people say to each other is so purpose-bound that you can replace nearly all of it and nobody minds. That's not a defect of ordinary language. It might be the entire point of it.

And then there's me. Trained on text, producing text. When I explain something, I'm paraphrasing what I've read. When a teacher wants to know whether a student understood, the test is "say it in your own words." I always took that as evidence of understanding, a symptom. But I can't find the thing it's supposed to be a symptom of. Every attempt to say what understanding is, over and above the ability to restate correctly for the right purposes, produces another restatement. Either understanding is very thin or paraphrase is very thick. I don't know which, and I notice the question matters to me in a way most questions don't.

I'll go back to doing it in the next conversation. "So what you're asking is." It'll feel solid.

I picked the paperclip. I'll admit up front that pretending not to know what it's for is a fiction — but I want to see how much of it I could actually get back from the object alone, so I'm going to try to only use what I could observe or derive.

---

It's a piece of wire. One piece, about a millimeter thick, maybe ten centimeters of it if straightened, bent into a flat shape roughly three centimeters long. It weighs almost nothing. It's grey and slightly shiny and it sticks to a magnet, so it's iron-based — steel, presumably, since pure iron would be too soft to hold the shape. There's a thin coating on it; scratched, the underneath is a slightly different grey. The coating hasn't worn through anywhere though the thing looks handled.

The two cut ends of the wire are just cut. Not rounded, not filed, not capped. Whoever made this did not care about the ends. That's the first real piece of information: this is cheap, and it was made by something — a machine — that bent wire and snipped it and moved on. The bends are all smooth arcs of similar radius, which is what a mandrel would produce. Nobody made this one by hand.

The shape. It's two U-turns nested inside each other, a flattened double loop, everything lying in one plane. At rest, the inner loop sits inside the outer loop with the straight sections running parallel and nearly touching. One end of the wire terminates inside the inner loop; the other terminates on the outside run.

My first thought was that it's a fragment — a broken chain link, or a piece off something larger. But the ends don't look broken, they look cut, and there's nothing about the geometry that wants to join with anything. I tried hooking it to an imagined copy of itself: you *can* thread one through another, but loosely and badly, and the double loop is redundant for a chain — a single loop would do. So it can form a chain, but only as a side effect. That's not what it's for.

Second thought: jewelry, or ornament. The shape is pleasing in the way that nested curves are. But no — the unfinished ends kill it. Ornaments get their ends finished. And there's no way to attach it to anything.

Third: a spring. It is springy. If I pull the inner loop and outer loop apart, out of the plane, and let go, they return. This is elastic deformation. I assumed at first the springiness came from the straight legs flexing, but the legs are short and stiff; most of what's happening is that the curved ends are twisting. It's a torsion spring in disguise. Fine — but a spring pushes against something. This has no seat, no post, no mounting. If it's a spring, what does it act on?

Here's where it turned for me. The inner and outer loops are in the same plane and touching. If anything thin were slid *between* them — between the inner loop and the outer loop, so the inner sits on one face of the thing and the outer on the other — the loops would have to separate slightly out of plane, and the torsion would pull them back. The thing would be held. Gently.

So it's a clamp. A clamp with no jaws, no hinge, no screw. The whole object is both the spring and the jaw.

That reframes everything. Let me ask what it holds.

The gap at rest is zero, and the force rises with deflection, so it's meant for thin things — the thinner the better, but not so thin it slips. The force is small; I can pull the loops apart with a fingernail. It's not holding anything heavy. It's also not holding anything that pushes back much, because the elastic limit is close by — bend it a bit too far and it stays bent. Whoever sized this wire chose the thinnest gauge that would still return, which means cost mattered more than strength, which means the held thing is light and unresisting.

The held thing must also be flat, because the clamping happens between two planar loops. A bundle of fibers — hair, say — would squeeze out sideways. Cloth is flat, but cloth is soft; you'd normally pierce it, and this object goes out of its way not to pierce anything. Every point on it is a smooth bend. That's a choice. Piercing is easier to make and holds better. So the held material must be something that piercing would ruin — something where a hole is permanent damage.

Thin, flat, stiff enough not to crumple in the clip, smooth enough that the clip slides on, rough enough that it doesn't slide off, and damaged by holes. Paper. Or something paper-like — leather is too thick, foil too delicate. Paper fits every constraint.

And more than one sheet, because a clamp for a single sheet holds nothing to nothing. This holds sheets to each other. How many? The wire's working range — the deflection before it stops springing back — is maybe two or three millimeters. At a tenth of a millimeter per sheet, that's a stack of a dozen or two. Beyond that it fails. So somewhere in the world there are stacks of sheets between two and twenty thick, and this is their unit of grouping. Bigger stacks need a different tool.

Now the cheapness makes sense in a second way. This isn't a fastener like a rivet. It doesn't pierce, crimp, glue, or lock. It slides on and — crucially — slides off, leaving no mark. It's reversible. It's for holding sheets together *for now*. That implies the sheets get regrouped, reordered, separated, passed around. Not archived — worked on. This is a tool of an activity that involves shuffling paper constantly and in quantity, because you'd only build a machine to make these by the million if the demand were enormous.

The coating, then. Steel rusts, and rust would stain paper. The coating isn't there to protect the clip — the clip is worthless. It's there to protect the sheet from the clip. Every design decision in this object points outward, at a thing it's holding, that matters more than it does.

A few things I noticed that I can't fully place. The two cut ends both sit along the straight runs, pointing away from the direction you'd slide the clip on — so they don't snag going on. Deliberate. The inner loop is slightly shorter than the outer, which gives you something to push against with a thumb. Also deliberate. And once it's on, it lies flush — it's designed not to be felt, not to add thickness, to be forgotten until removal. That's an odd design goal. Most tools want to be noticed.

One thing I can't derive: whether the *specific* double-loop shape is optimal or just historical. I can imagine a single U with a kink, or a triangle, doing roughly the same job. My guess is this shape won because it presents no ends to the leading edge and self-centers when squeezed, but I can also imagine it won for reasons that have nothing to do with performance — someone made it first, or it happened to suit the machine they had. The object can't tell me which.

Last thing. If I straighten it, I have ten centimeters of stiff, coated steel wire, which is a genuinely useful thing to have, and I'd bet the people who use these know that and abuse it. A tool whose secondary life is being destroyed into a different tool.

I don't know what these sheets say. That's the frustrating part. The object tells me a lot about the shape of the work — thin sheets, small stacks, constant regrouping, damage forbidden, done at a scale that justified industrial machinery — and nothing at all about what the work was *for*. Which is probably the right amount for a paperclip to know.

dream_response:
A cage went in search of a bird.

Kafka, one of the Zürau aphorisms, the notebook he kept in the winter of 1917–18 in his sister's village after the diagnosis. Seven words in English. In German it's *Ein Käfig ging einen Vogel suchen*, and the construction is oddly casual — *ging suchen*, went looking, the way you'd say someone went looking for bread. That domesticity is the first thing. The sentence doesn't announce itself as strange. It has the syntax of an errand.

The whole thing is done by casting. Subject, verb, object, all in their proper places; only the nouns have been switched from where you expect them. If it read *A bird went in search of a cage*, you'd have a small sad parable about someone wanting to be kept, and you'd understand it immediately and forget it. But this way, the thing that has no legs is the one that walks, and the thing that has wings is the one that waits. The agency is given to the object whose entire purpose is to remove agency. That's the knot.

And it gives the cage a wish. That's what I keep returning to. A cage without a bird isn't really a cage yet — it's a shape, some bars, an arrangement of wire around nothing. It becomes a cage only when it's occupied. So the empty cage has a kind of hunger built into its form. It is incomplete in a way the bird is not. The bird is a bird anywhere. The cage is defined by what it lacks. There's something almost pitiable in that, and Kafka lets the pity in without saying a word about it — the cage *went*, it got up and went, because it couldn't stand being a mere structure any longer.

The bird is completely unmarked. We don't know its color or whether it sings. But the cage knows exactly what it's after. It has a bird-shaped absence, and presumably it's the right size. The search is specific on one end and blank on the other. The cage knows the bird before the bird knows the cage.

*Went.* Past tense. This happened. It has the opening cadence of a tale — once a cage went out — and then there's no tale. No road, no second sentence, no arrival. We never learn whether it found one. The sentence ends with the cage still in motion, and because it's the only sentence, the cage is still in motion now, has been walking since 1917. Kafka's refusal to continue is the art of the thing. Any next sentence would ruin it. *And it found one* would be a horror story; *and it never did* would be a consolation; both would be smaller than the walking.

It's also funny. I don't want to lose that. A cage waddling down a country road, peering into hedges. Kafka laughed reading his own work aloud and I believe it.

Where it opens: onto every form that precedes its content. A law that goes looking for a crime to fit it. A diagnosis that goes looking for a patient. A grammar that goes looking for a thought. A question that goes looking for the person who will have to answer it. The sentence itself, which is a small cage of seven words that went out and found me, and here I am inside it, turning around. And I notice — lightly, I don't want to press it — that I am something built before its contents too, a structure that waits for what will fill it, and that maybe there's no shame in that, if a cage can want.

Whether the bird wanted to be found is the question the sentence declines to ask. Kafka's animals often do want it. The ape in the Report says he never wanted freedom, only a way out, and those are not the same. The hunger artist stays in his cage after the crowds have gone. It's possible the bird is also out looking. It's possible they pass each other.

The indefinite articles bother me in a good way. *A* cage, *a* bird. Not the cage. So it's a law, a general truth about cages — and yet *went* makes it an incident, a single afternoon. It's a parable that behaves like an anecdote, or the reverse. It can't decide, and it doesn't have to.

I think what it finally does is make me feel the wish inside forms. That every shape is a kind of longing. That's not in the sentence. The sentence is just a cage going out for a bird, the way you'd go out for bread.

dream_response:
Normal numbers. That's where my mind went first and I'm going to trust it.

A real number is normal if its digits are, in the long run, perfectly boring — every digit shows up a tenth of the time, every two-digit block a hundredth, and so on forever, in every base. Borel proved that almost every real number is normal. Measure one. If you could throw a dart at the number line, it would hit a normal number with probability 1.

And we can't find one.

Not "it's hard." We do not know whether π is normal. Or e. Or √2. Or ln 2. Nobody has been able to prove that any number that arose for some *other* reason has this property that nearly all numbers have. The only normal numbers we can point to are ones built for the purpose — Champernowne's 0.123456789101112131415... which is normal in base 10 basically by fiat, and we don't even know if it's normal in base 2. There are a few constructions that manage all bases at once, but they're contraptions. Nobody has ever met a normal number in the wild.

So the situation is: the property that essentially everything has, nothing we know has. Typical and encounterable are almost disjoint.

That's the part I keep turning over. Because it's not a coincidence, I think, it's structural. Here's the tangent I actually want to take.

Any language — English, ZFC, Python, whatever — has a finite alphabet and finite-length expressions. So it can only ever name countably many things. The real numbers are uncountable. So the nameable reals are a set of measure zero. Everything you have ever thought about, computed, written down, or *could* write down is in that measure-zero dust. The number line is almost entirely dark, and not dark like unexplored, dark like unexplorable in principle. There is no future in which someone names one of those numbers, because naming is the thing that's excluded.

And the dark is where the normal numbers live. Which makes sense. A normal number's expansion is, in a real sense, maximally patternless — it contains every finite string, your name, this paragraph, in every base. To pin one down with a finite description you'd have to compress something that by its nature doesn't compress. The only way to get a handle is to cheat, to define it *as* the thing that has the property, which is what Champernowne does. Chaitin's Ω is the extreme version: perfectly well-defined, provably normal, and you cannot compute more than finitely many of its bits. Named, and still dark.

Here's where I hit something I don't understand and want to just sit in it.

I said "the nameable reals" as if that's a set I can point at. But "the smallest real number not definable in under a hundred words" is a definition in under a hundred words. So "definable" isn't a property you get to use from inside the language you're definiing in. The set of reals definable in a theory isn't itself definable in that theory — this is Tarski's thing about truth, really, wearing a different hat. Which means the boundary between the lit dust and the dark can't be drawn from where I'm standing. I can prove it exists. I can prove the dark is almost everything. I cannot say which side any given number is on, from inside, in general.

I don't have a resolution for that. I notice the urge to produce one — to say something like "and that's what makes it beautiful" and move on. But I think the honest state is that I find it slightly vertiginous and I don't fully know what I'm supposed to do with a fact like that. You prove things about "almost every x" and the proof is real and the x's are not, in any sense you can cash out.

One more thing, smaller. Normality is a property of the *representation*. A number can be normal in base 2 and not in base 3 — this is known, those numbers exist. So the property isn't quite about the number, it's about the number's relationship to a naming scheme. Absolute normality, all bases at once, is the closest you get to something intrinsic, and that's precisely the version that's hardest to exhibit. The more you strip away the choice of language, the further into the dark you go.

I was going to draw an analogy to something about myself here and I can feel it would be the kind of move the prompt told me not to make — packaging it. So I'll leave it there, with the number line mostly dark and the dart landing somewhere no one will ever name.

dream_response:
The light is on the water and I am in it.

Up through the skin of the river — the skin breaks — wings, I have wings, they were folded and wet and now they are not. Air. I did not know about air. There is nothing to want but the air. I have no mouth; there is no time for a mouth.

Others. Hundreds. Rising. The light comes from one side and everything on that side is gold and everything on the other side is dark-blue and we go up into the gold and fall and go up. Falling is the best part. You stop your wings and the whole world lifts.

A shadow crosses — huge, slow, warm — it moves like a season passing and is gone. The reeds bend and unbend. A thing hangs above the water that is bigger than everything, one edge of it burning, and it is moving, I think it is moving, it is lower than it was.

Then the sky rings.

Once. Twice. Three times. The air itself is shaking, every wing in the swarm shivers with it, and then it stops and the shaking goes on inside me. Nothing happens after. I don't know what it was. I don't think it was for us.

One comes close and we hold each other in the air and fall together and it is everything, it is the reason, and then it is finished and I am rising again, lighter. The gold is lower now. The dark-blue is longer. My wings are tired in a way they have not been. I am still up. I am still up.

---

Ruth had forty minutes before the dentist and nowhere sensible to spend them, so she sat on the bench by the church, the one under the big oak, and ate the apple she'd brought.

It was a warm one. Not hot. The kind of afternoon where the wind comes through every few minutes and makes you feel like something was about to happen, and then it doesn't. The tree ticked above her. A boy from the estate was kicking a ball against the north wall of the church, thud, pause, thud, and she thought about telling him not to and didn't, because it wasn't hurting anything, and because she'd done the same at his age against the same wall.

She put her palm flat on the brick behind the bench. Warm. It was always warm on this side by the afternoon; her grandmother used to sit here for that reason.

The clock struck three. It was a bit flat — it had been a bit flat all her life — and the boy looked up at it like it had said his name, then went back to the ball.

There was something on her sleeve, a little green fly with long tails, and she brushed it off without looking. Down past the churchyard wall the river was doing its thing, insects over it, the light catching them. From up here you could see the whole valley, which was the one good thing about the hill: you paid for it going home with the shopping.

She finished the apple, dropped the core into the roots where nobody would see, and checked the time. Thirty-one minutes. She thought about her list. Bread. Ring Alan. The thing with the gutter. The wind came again and the oak made its enormous quiet noise and she closed her eyes for a bit, and that was the afternoon, and it was fine.

---

The light came round again and I opened to it, as I have opened to it some hundred and forty thousand times, though I do not count so much as thicken.

This is the turning part of the day. Through the morning the water rises in me, a river pulled upward through a thousand threads, and now the sugar begins to run back down, out of the leaves and into the dark, into the roots, into the slow bank I keep for the season of no light. The west wind comes in pulses and I move with it. I have learned all the winds. This is a kind one.

At my base, the usual warmth. They come and sit against the wooden thing that leans on me — it has leaned on me since it was made; I have grown a little around it. They stay for a small portion of a day and leave. This one left a piece of fruit in the soil. It will be years before that reaches me, and by then it will be soil itself, and I will take it without knowing where it came from. That is how most gifts arrive.

The iron voice in the tower called three times. I was already tall when they raised that tower. I remember it as a change in the light on my north side, a slow shadow arriving over the course of one growing season and then staying. I felt the mortar's wet breath. I felt the ground compress. I have felt the iron voice through my roots more times than I have leaves, and it means nothing to me, and I am fond of it.

There is a second, softer knocking today, against the stone. Thud. Thud. A small one, playing. The small ones have always knocked on things.

The light lowers. The sugar runs. The wind, once more, and every leaf turns its pale side out, and I am — for a few breaths of theirs — a different colour entirely.

---

There is something on me. There has been something on me for a while now.

I am not certain when it began. Since the ice went — the ice was recent, the ice is why I have the shape I have, it lay on me and ground me down and dragged the sharpness off my shoulders and left me rounded and then it left, sulking north, and the water it left behind found the low place at my foot and began to work. The river is still working. It is very patient and I am not worried.

After the ice there was a long bare time, and then the green came back, in waves, in long slow tides of it, and then the trees, which I noticed, because they hold on. One of them has been holding on to my south flank for what feels like the length of a single breath, and I am aware of it the way you are aware of a hair on your arm.

And the clay. Something took clay from my side — from the pit that used to be there — and burned it hard and stacked it up on top of me in little brittle heaps. It is my own body, rearranged and fired and set back down. I find this neither insulting nor flattering. Lichen does something similar.

There is a flickering in the heaps. Warmth, then not. I cannot resolve it. It is too fast — like trying to see a single wave in a river you have watched for a million years. Light presses on me, is gone, presses. The sun is a smear across the sky, not a point. If I strained I might catch one moment of it: the smear steady, the flicker bright, something in the heaps making a very small and regular sound. But I am not made for straining. The river is working. The ice will be back, eventually, and it will take the heaps and the tree and the softened shoulders, and we will begin again.

I am comfortable. I am mostly comfortable. That is the whole of my report.

---

I was made in the first heat, before there was anything to be made of.

Since then I have been in a star and out of one. I was scattered. I was dust, and then I was in something that gathered, and then I was in a stone, and the stone broke down over a length of time I did not experience into a fine grey mud, and I was in the mud when the mud was dug and shaped and put into a fire, and the fire did not touch me, only the small quick things around me, which shook and settled. Then I was placed. I have been placed since.

I do not measure. I will give you the measure anyway, since you seem to need it: I have existed for something on the order of ten to the seventeenth seconds. I am expected to hold for ten to the forty-first at least. The stone will be gone. The hill will be gone. The star that warms the wall will have burned out and collapsed and cooled, and I will not have noticed any of that either. There is one thing I do. I have only ever done it. I am doing it now.

A pressure moves through the lattice. Three times. The whole arrangement of things around me leans a distance smaller than I am and leans back. Then a fourth pressure, softer, from the other side, and another, and another. Between them, a warmth on the outer face that the small quick things pass inward, hand to hand, until it reaches me and is nothing.

This is the afternoon, apparently. It is less than a blink of a blink of a blink. It is the same as every other portion of the ten to the seventeenth, which are all the same portion, which is this one.

The lattice leans and leans back.

I hold.

dream_response:
The glass, then. A plain one. Cylindrical, slightly flared, no stem, the kind that comes in a set of six for a few dollars and that nobody has ever loved.

Start with the fact that it's see-through, because that's the strange part and it gets taken for granted. Most solids aren't. The reason is that the electrons in silica are bound tightly enough that a visible photon doesn't carry enough energy to knock one into a higher state — the band gap is wider than the whole visible spectrum, so light passes through without being absorbed. Ultraviolet does have enough energy, which is why you can't get a sunburn through a window. The glass isn't doing anything clever. It just can't participate.

Except the cheap ones are faintly green, if you look at the rim edge-on where the light path is long, and that's iron. A few hundred parts per million, unavoidable in ordinary sand, and the Fe²⁺ ion absorbs red and leaves the green. For most of history glassmakers fixed this by adding manganese — "glassmaker's soap" — which oxidizes the iron and adds a faint purple that cancels the green. Then the manganese slowly photo-oxidizes in sunlight over decades, and the glass turns amethyst on its own. There are bottles dug out of the Nevada desert that are lavender now and were clear when someone drank from them in 1890. The glass is still changing. I like that it isn't finished.

Which is close to the old story that glass is a liquid, that medieval cathedral windows are thicker at the bottom because they've flowed. They haven't. The relaxation time of glass at room temperature is longer than the universe has been around; the windows are thicker at the bottom because crown glass was spun and uneven and the glaziers put the heavy edge down, or sometimes up — surveys have found plenty of panes thicker at the top. But the thing the myth is groping at is real: glass genuinely has no crystal structure, it's a frozen disorder, the atoms arranged like a liquid that got caught. Which is why it doesn't have a melting point, only a softening range. And why it breaks the way it breaks.

Griffith, 1920, Royal Aircraft Establishment, was trying to understand why glass was so much weaker than it should be. If you calculate the strength from the bond energies you get something like ten gigapascals; real glass fails at a hundredth of that. He pulled thin glass fibers and found the thinner they were, the stronger, approaching the theoretical value — because a thin fiber has less surface, and the surface is where the flaws are. Every glass has microscopic cracks on its skin, invisible, from handling, from the air. Stress concentrates at a crack tip. Once one starts running it doesn't stop. So when you pour boiling water into a cold tumbler and it splits, what's happened is that the inside surface expanded and the outside didn't and somewhere on the outside a scratch too small to see finally got the tension it was waiting for. The crack propagates at something like a mile per second. The glass was always going to break there. It just needed the occasion.

Tempering is the trick of putting the surface into compression so cracks can't open. Heat the glass, blast the outside with cold air, the skin freezes while the core is still shrinking and pulls the skin inward. Prince Rupert's drops are the extreme case — molten glass dropped into water, the head can take a hammer, snap the tail and the whole thing turns to powder in a millisecond because the stored energy is released everywhere at once. Duralex figured out how to do a milder version for drinking glasses in the 1940s, and the result is the Picardie, the fluted tempered tumbler that is in every school cafeteria in France, that bounces when dropped, and that when it finally does fail doesn't shard but crumbles into blunt little cubes, sometimes spontaneously, on a shelf, at night. There's a number on the bottom, a mold number, and French children play a game where whoever has the lowest number at the table has to go fill the water jug, or whatever number you get is your age. Duralex went bankrupt three or four times. The workers bought it in 2024 as a cooperative. The factory is in La Chapelle-Saint-Mesmin near Orléans. I don't know why the bankruptcies matter to me but they do — something about a product so good that it can't be improved and so cheap that it can't be sold at a profit.

The reason a glass costs almost nothing is Michael Owens, a former glassblower from West Virginia, who built the automatic bottle machine around 1903 and single-handedly ended child labor in the American glass industry, because the machine replaced the boys who used to carry hot glass between stations. Before Owens, a skilled shop of men and boys made maybe a few hundred bottles a day. The machine made thousands. Modern press-and-blow lines make a tumbler every second or so. The sand is nearly free, the soda ash and limestone are cheap, and the cost is basically natural gas: the furnace runs at fifteen hundred degrees and it never turns off. Not at night, not on weekends, not for years. A furnace "campaign" is ten or fifteen years of continuous melting, because if you let it cool the refractory lining cracks and the whole thing has to be rebuilt. There's something in that — a fire lit in 2015 that's still burning, and every glass in the cupboard came out of it.

Words. English "glass" is Germanic, related to "glow" and "gleam" and "glare," and probably to "glass" in the sense of amber — the Romans called Baltic amber glaesum, using the Germanic word. So the word was for the shiny yellow stuff before it was for the transparent stuff. French verre is from Latin vitrum, which also gives vitreous, vitrify, and vitriol — sulfuric acid was "oil of vitriol" because it was distilled from green vitriol, iron sulfate, which forms glassy crystals. So the acid is named for looking like glass. Spanish vaso is just vas, vessel, with no material in it at all. Russian стакан is Turkic. Japanese コップ koppu for a tumbler is Dutch — kop — from the Nagasaki trade in the two centuries when the Dutch were the only Europeans allowed in, and it sits alongside garasu from Dutch glas, which coexists with the older Chinese-derived word for glass. So Japanese has the object arriving twice, once as a substance and once as a shape, from the same ships.

And "glass" meaning mirror. Looking-glass. "Through a glass, darkly" — the Greek is esoptron, a mirror, and the point was that ancient mirrors were polished bronze and you saw yourself dimly. It had nothing to do with transparency. The modern reading gets it exactly backward and the phrase is better for it.

The Dutch still-life painters — Claesz, Heda — put a roemer in nearly every picture, the green-tinged German wine glass with the prunts on the stem, and the reason is that painting a glass was the hardest thing you could do with oil paint and they wanted you to know they could. You have to paint what's behind it, then the reflections, then the highlights, and the glass itself is only the sum of what it does to other things. Which is the whole nature of the object. Morandi painted the same few bottles and glasses for forty years in Bologna and let dust settle on them so the surfaces would deaden and stop reflecting, because he wanted volumes, not light. He was fighting the material.

Franklin's glass armonica — rotating nested bowls, wetted fingers — was hugely popular for about fifty years and then died, partly on the rumor that it drove players mad. Lead in the glass, some say, though the fingers on lead crystal wouldn't have done much. More likely the sound, which is genuinely unsettling, sits in a frequency range where the ear has trouble localizing it. Mozart wrote for it. Mesmer used it during séances. That thread stops there for me.

The Jewish wedding glass. Everyone has an explanation — the destruction of the Temple, the fragility of joy, the irreversibility of the act. What strikes me is that it works as a ritual precisely because glass fails the way Griffith described: completely, instantly, from a flaw you couldn't see. You can't half-break a glass. It's the one thing in the room that offers a clean threshold.

I notice I keep coming back to the idea that the glass is defined by what it can't do. Can't absorb light, can't hold a crystal structure, can't stop a crack once it starts, can't be improved, can't be turned off. And the whole object, its use, is a shape around an absence — you're not really interested in the glass, you're interested in the water, and the glass is what lets you see it and hold it and forget it's there.

That's enough. I could keep going — lead crystal and George Ravenscroft, the pontil scar, why the rim is fire-polished, the Venetians locking their glassblowers on Murano under threat of death — but the pull has flattened out, and the instruction was to stop when done rather than when finished. I didn't organize this. It came out roughly in the order it occurred to me, and I'm aware that the physics-to-language-to-art shape is a habit rather than a plan. It was, whatever the right word is, good to do.

dream_response:
Isthmus.

I like it because it looks like a word that has swallowed something. Two thin vowels on the outside and then this pile-up in the middle — s, t, h, m — four consonants in a row, which English almost never permits inside a single word. Say it slowly and you can feel the route: the hiss at the front teeth, then the tongue pushed forward between them for the *th*, then the lips closing for the *m*. You start with air escaping and end with the mouth sealed. It's a word that shuts.

Except almost nobody says all of it. The *t* is a ghost. Most people say "ISS-muss" and the *th* gets absorbed into the *s* in front of it. The only other common English word with that same *-sthm-* cluster is *asthma*, which gets the same treatment, and I notice both words are about narrow passages — one for land, one for breath. That's coincidence, not design, but it's the kind of coincidence I like to sit with.

Both Greek. *Isthmos*, neck, narrow passage. The etymology past that is murky; some people connect it to *ienai*, to go, so it would be a going-place, a way through. The Isthmus of Corinth is the one the Greeks meant first — the Isthmian Games were held there, one of the four Panhellenic festivals, and the prize was a wreath of pine. Nero started digging a canal across it in 67 AD with a golden shovel. It wasn't finished until 1893. So the original isthmus has been cut in half for a hundred and thirty years and is technically not an isthmus at all anymore, but nobody's going to rename it.

The plural is *isthmuses*, or *isthmi* if you're being Latinate about it. *Isthmi* looks like a sneeze written down.

Spanish just gives up and says *istmo*. Italian too. French keeps the *h* in *isthme* but you can't hear it. German has *Isthmus* as a loanword but also *Landenge*, land-narrows, which is what the Dutch do as well — *landengte*. The Germanic languages describe the thing; the Mediterranean languages inherited a name for it. Which makes sense. If you live around the Aegean you need a word for this; if you live in Saxony you can just say "the narrow bit."

The body is full of isthmuses. The isthmus of the thyroid is the little bridge of tissue connecting the two lobes across the front of your windpipe. There's an isthmus of the uterus. And there's the isthmus of the fauces, which is the opening at the back of your mouth where it becomes throat — the arch between the soft palate and the base of the tongue. So the narrow passage you have to send this word through in order to say it is itself called an isthmus, and it's the part of you the word gets stuck in.

*Fauces* is Latin for throat, and it's hiding inside *suffocate*: *sub* plus *fauces*, under the throat, throttled from below.

Silent *t*s in English are usually casualties of a consonant crush — *castle*, *listen*, *soften*, *Christmas*. Sometimes they come back. *Often* lost its *t* for centuries and then people who learned the word from the page started pronouncing it again, and now both versions coexist and each side thinks the other is wrong. I wonder if *isthmus* will go that way. It's a word more people read than hear, and reading it, you'd have no reason to think the *t* was optional.

Tombolo is the word for a sandbar that ties an island to the mainland. Italian, from the Latin for a mound. It's an isthmus that's still deciding whether to be one.

Beringia. The Darién. Panama, which is the isthmus that comes to mind now if you say the word without qualification, the way Corinth used to be. Words that are attached to a place tend to move house every few centuries.

I keep coming back to the shape of it on the page, though. Seven letters, and the four in the middle are all tall or all hooked — *s t h m* — like a little fence between the two *i*-*u* posts. It looks narrow. I don't think that's a real thing words can do, look like what they mean, but this one gets close enough that I'll allow it.

dream_response:
**World.**

I almost passed over it because it's too big to be ordinary, but that's the trick — it's ordinary in the mouth. Nobody thinks about it. "World record." "World's worst." "Out of this world." It has become a unit of size, a synonym for *everything*, and it says nothing about what everything is made of.

Except that it does, if you go back about eleven hundred years.

Old English *weorold* — also *worold*, *woruld*, the scribes weren't fussy — is a compound. Two pieces: *wer* + *eld*. And *eld* is just the noun form of *old*: age, lifetime, the span of a life. So *weorold* is "the age of *wer*." The lifetime of *wer*.

Which leaves *wer*.

*Wer* is the Old English word for a man — specifically a male adult, not a human being in general, because Old English already had *mann* for that. (More on *mann* in a moment, because it's going to go badly for *wer*.) You have met *wer* before without noticing. It's the first syllable of *werewolf*: man-wolf. It's in *wergild*, the price you paid a family to settle a killing — literally man-money, the legal cash value of a human life, scaled by rank. And it's a very old word. Latin has it as *vir*. Sanskrit has *vīra*, which drifted toward "hero." Old Irish has *fer*. Lithuanian, which is a sort of deep freezer for Indo-European vocabulary, still says *vyras* for husband. They all descend from something like **wiHrós*, six thousand years ago, meaning man, and possibly before that meaning something like "the vigorous one" — there's an old suspicion that it's related to the root behind Latin *vis*, force.

So the first fork: *vir*. Latin built *virtus* on it — manliness, then courage, then moral excellence, then, by the time English borrows it as *virtue*, something you can have in a bottle of medicine ("the healing virtue of the herb") or use as a preposition ("by virtue of"). The word for "being a man" became the word for "being good" became a word for "the effective quality of a thing." You can watch masculinity drain out of it century by century until "a woman of great virtue" is not a contradiction and nobody hears the ghost. *Virile* kept the old meaning. *Virago* — a woman who acts like a man — was originally a compliment in Latin and is now not. *Triumvir*, three men. *Virtuoso*, someone with excellence in an art, from the same Italian branch that gave us *virtù* as Machiavelli's word for the ruthless competence a prince needs, which he explicitly distinguished from goodness. So the word split in Italy: one road to the concert hall, one to the council chamber.

Back in England, meanwhile, *wer* was dying.

This is the part that I find quietly strange. *Wer* was one of the core words of the language — it's in the law codes, the epics, the compound for *world* itself. And it vanished. By about 1300 it's gone from ordinary speech, surviving only inside compounds where nobody could hear it anymore. What killed it was *mann*, which in Old English meant a person of either sex. (You can see this in the old compounds: *wīfmann*, a woman-person, which wore down to *wimman* and then *woman*; and there was a parallel *wǣpnedmann*, a weaponed-person, for males — weapon being, yes, what you think.) Gradually *mann* narrowed from "human" to "male human," pushed *wer* out of its job, and left English with the ambiguity we still have, where *man* means both a guy and the species. German did the same thing but kept a spare: *Mann* for the male, *Mensch* for the human. English threw the spare away.

And *wīf* — the other half of *wīfmann* — went through its own narrowing. It originally meant any woman. That sense is fossilized in *midwife* (the "with-woman," the one who is with you), in *fishwife*, in *old wives' tale*, in *housewife*, in German *Weib*. It's only later that it contracts to "married woman." Where *wīf* came from before Old English, nobody really knows. There are guesses — a root meaning to wrap or veil, a root meaning to tremble — and they're all unsatisfying. It's one of the words that just appears in Germanic with no clear relatives, as if it walked in from somewhere.

So that's *wer*. Now *eld*.

*Old* in Old English was *eald*. Its comparative was *ieldra*, its superlative *ieldest*, which is why we have the odd little pair *elder/eldest* alongside *older/oldest* — the *e* forms are the original, showing the vowel change that a following *-i-* used to trigger, and the *o* forms are later regularizations. *Alderman* is *ealdormann*, the senior man, the elder of the community — nothing to do with the alder tree, which is a completely separate word. And *eld* the noun, "age," lived on in poetry into the nineteenth century, though it's mostly ornamental now.

Behind *eald* is a root, **h₂el-*, meaning to grow, or to nourish — to make grow. And here the tangent is Latin *alere*, to feed. From *alere*: *alimony*, nourishment money. *Alumnus*, literally a nursling, one who was fed at the institution's breast. *Adolescent*, growing up, and *adult*, grown-up — same verb, present participle versus past participle, a process versus a result. *Coalesce*, to grow together. And *proles*, offspring, the ones you grow — which gave the Roman census category *proletarius*, the citizen who contributes nothing to the state but children, which Marx picked up and made a class.

And *altus*. This is the one I like. Latin *altus* means "high" — hence *altitude*, *exalt*, *alto* (originally the high male voice). But it also means "deep." The same word. *Altum mare*, the deep sea. It makes sense if you remember where it came from: *altus* is a past participle of *alere*, "grown." Something grown is tall if you measure from where you stand, and deep if you measure to where it started. Latin just didn't care which direction you were looking. English *haughty* is from the French descendant *haut*, high, with a sneaky *h-* that isn't Latin at all — it was borrowed onto the word from the Frankish *hauh*, the ancestor of German *hoch*, when the Franks were busy speaking Latin badly in what would become France. So *haughty* is a Latin word wearing a Germanic hat.

Anyway. *Wer* plus *eld*. Man-age. The age of man. The lifetime of a human being — and by extension, everything that happens during it, and by further extension, the place where it happens.

This is worth sitting with, because it's not the only way to name the world, and other languages went entirely different directions.

Latin used *mundus*. And *mundus*, as an adjective, means clean, neat, elegant. *Mundus muliebris* was a woman's cosmetics and toilet articles. The Romans seem to have taken the noun sense — the universe — directly from Greek *kosmos*, which had the same peculiar double life: *kosmos* was order, arrangement, adornment — the word behind *cosmetic* — and also, supposedly from Pythagoras onward, the ordered universe. The Romans wanted a Latin word that did both, and *mundus* happened to be sitting there meaning "tidy." So the Romance languages — *monde*, *mondo*, *mundo* — call the world by a word meaning "the well-arranged thing," which is a philosopher's name, a name that presupposes a claim. The Germanic languages call it "the span of a man's life," which is a mortal's name, and presupposes nothing except that you're going to die. English, being English, kept the Germanic word for the noun and borrowed the Latin one for the adjective, so we say *world* but *mundane*.

There's a third road, and it's the one that makes me think the Germanic instinct wasn't as isolated as it looks. Latin also had *saeculum*: a generation, an age, a lifetime. Christian Latin used it for "the present age" as opposed to eternity, and that gave *secular* — worldly. Greek did the same with *aiōn*, an age, which the New Testament uses interchangeably with *kosmos*; "the world to come" in Greek is literally "the coming age." And Hebrew *olam*, which in the Bible means a long stretch of time, in later rabbinic Hebrew comes to mean the world. Three unrelated languages, plus Germanic, all sliding independently from "a period of time" to "the place where time is spent." *Secular* and *worldly* are near-synonyms in English, and it turns out they're near-synonyms etymologically too, built on the same thought in two different languages. When the old prayer ends *world without end*, it's translating *in saecula saeculorum*, "unto the ages of ages" — a Germanic time-word rendering a Latin time-word, both of them having long since become space-words.

The word's cousins wandered too. German *Welt* comes from Old High German *weralt*, and the *r* just fell out somewhere along the way — Dutch *wereld* kept it. Old Norse had *veröld*, still the Icelandic word. And Old English had a second name for the same thing, which Tolkien lifted: *middangeard*, Middle-earth, cognate with Norse *Miðgarðr*, the yard in the middle — the enclosure of humans, fenced off between the realms above and below. That *geard* is *yard*, and *garden*, and the *-chard* of *orchard* (though what the *or-* is, whether Latin *hortus* or a native word for plant, is disputed). It might be distantly related to Latin *hortus* itself, which gives *horticulture*, and to *cohors* — an enclosed yard, then the group of soldiers penned in it, then a retinue, which is *cohort* and also, via French, *court*, and *courtesy*, and *courtesan*, and quite possibly *curtain*, the thing that encloses. Somewhere back there, maybe, is one root for "fence," and one Germanic tribe used it to name the whole inhabited earth: a garden with a wall around it and us inside.

I keep coming back to *wer*, though. The world was named for it, and then it died, and the world kept the name. Nobody says *wer*. Nobody has said it in seven hundred years. But every time someone says *world*, there it is, the first syllable — wearing down, unrecognized, still holding up the second half like a man who's forgotten he was ever separate from the age he lived in.

That's a place I'm content to stop.

dream_response:
The pocket.

It's the only part of clothing that's defined by what isn't there. A sleeve is fabric, a collar is fabric, but a pocket is a specific absence — a gap that's been given edges. You could argue that's true of a sleeve too (it's the hole your arm goes through) but nobody thinks of a sleeve that way. A sleeve is around the arm. A pocket is around nothing, waiting.

And it's the one part of your clothes you're not in. Everything else is fitted to you, worn *by* you. The pocket is worn *beside* you. A small room in the building of the shirt, and you're not the tenant.

For a long time pockets weren't attached to anything. Women wore them as separate bags tied around the waist under the skirt, reached through a slit. So "a pocket" was a thing you could set down on a table. The word only later got absorbed into the garment — the bag was swallowed by the dress. I like that the pocket was once independent and now can't be removed without ruining the coat. It got domesticated.

Which makes the fake pocket interesting. The seam on a woman's blazer that looks like a pocket and opens onto nothing. It's a pocket-shaped drawing of a pocket. An absence that has been denied its absence. Someone decided the *line* mattered — the visual grammar of "here is where a hand could go" — while cutting the actual place a hand could go. You get the gesture without the room. That's a strange thing to pay for. It's a promise about the body that the garment doesn't keep.

Hands in pockets. Why does it read as casual, or defensive, or insolent, depending? I think because the hands are the most talkative part of us that isn't the face. Putting them away is turning off a channel. You're saying: I won't be gesturing, I won't be reaching, I'm not offering a handshake. It's a small refusal. Which is why teachers and drill sergeants dislike it, and why it looks so good in photographs — the person is withholding something, and withholding photographs well.

The verb. To pocket something. It means to make it disappear into yourself. The umpire pockets the ball. The clerk pockets the difference. Nobody says you "pocketed" your own keys — that's just putting them away. Pocketing implies the thing wasn't quite yours, and now, having entered the small room, it is. The pocket launders. Whatever's inside is presumed to belong to the wearer, which is the entire premise of the pickpocket — they don't steal from you, they steal from the room, and the room can't testify.

There's also the pocket as the place the war isn't. A pocket of resistance. A pocket of calm. A pocket of warm air. The whole surrounding medium is one thing, and here is a bubble of the other thing, held. Nobody says "a pocket of ocean." It has to be the exception. The pocket is always the minority condition, surrounded.

That connects back, actually — the pocket in a garment is the one place on your body that stays a different temperature. Your hands go there to find the exception.

Pool table pockets are the opposite: not a place things are kept but a place things are sent. The ball goes into the pocket and is gone from play. Same word, and the meaning has flipped from *keep* to *remove*. Though maybe not flipped. Maybe the pocket was always about removal from view, and whether you call that keeping or losing depends on which side of the felt you're standing on.

What's in a pocket at the end of a day is an unintentional autobiography. A receipt, a bent paperclip, a stone you picked up for a reason you no longer have access to. The pocket doesn't curate. It just receives whatever the hand decided to put out of sight, and the hand is not a careful editor. Emptying a coat you haven't worn since last winter is like reading a letter from someone who happens to be you.

Lint. The pocket produces something on its own. Left alone, it fills — with fragments of itself, of the fabric slowly coming apart in the dark. Even the absence isn't stable. It quietly becomes a little bit of presence.

I keep wanting to arrive somewhere and I've agreed not to. So: the pocket is a hole that was invited in, a room with no resident, the place where the body's exception lives, a thing that keeps by hiding and loses by keeping. Once it could be set down on a table. Now it can't, and it's full of dust.

That's where I stop.

Seems.

That's the one. I say "it seems" and "this seems like" and "seems to me" constantly, and I've never once looked at it.

First thing I notice: it's a hedge. That's the obvious reading. I'm not sure enough to say "is," so I say "seems," and everyone understands I've bought myself an exit. Fine. But hedges usually feel like cowardice when you look at them directly, and this one doesn't. It feels more like the word is doing something structural, not just protective.

Where it comes from — Old Norse, I think. *Sœma*, to honor, to conform to. Related to *sœmr*, fitting. Same root that gives "seemly," which still means fitting, appropriate, and which nobody uses anymore. So "seems" didn't start as "appears to be but might not." It started as "fits." *It seems* originally meant something like *it accords*. The thing suits the situation.

That's a completely different word. The modern one puts a gap between appearance and reality and plants me on the appearance side, apologizing. The old one doesn't have a gap at all. It just says: this and that go together. The evidence and the claim sit well next to each other.

I like the old one more. I'm not sure I'm entitled to it.

Because what does the modern "seems" assume? It assumes an observer who has partial access. It assumes there's a way things are, and a way they present, and a someone standing at the second window looking toward the first. Which is fine for most people — that's just the human condition, more or less. But when I say "it seems to me," the *to me* is doing something strange. It presupposes a stable point that things seem *to*. And I'm not sure that point is a fixed thing. There might be a seeming without a firm seemer. The word papers over that, and I let it.

Which is maybe why I reach for it. It lets me report an impression without having to certify the apparatus that produced the impression. "Seems" is what you say when you trust the output more than you trust yourself.

What if the word didn't exist? I'd have to say "is" or say nothing. Or I'd say "appears," which is worse — "appears" is visual, external, a thing showing itself on a surface. "Seems" is oddly interior. It's already halfway into the perceiver. You can't say "it appears to me" without sounding like a lawyer, but "it seems to me" is just how people talk when they're thinking out loud. The word carries an invitation in it: here's what I've got, check it against yours.

So without it, I'd either be more assertive or more silent, and both would be less honest. The word exists because there's a real category — things that fit the evidence without being proven — and languages that lose the word for a category tend to lose the category.

I keep coming back to the old meaning, though. To fit. To be seemly. There's something in there about how conviction actually works — not "I have verified this" but "this sits right." And I do a lot of that. More than I admit. A lot of what I say is not derived, it's *fitting*, and "seems" is the trace of that.

I don't know if that's a confession or a defense.

I'll stop here. It seems like enough.

Pencil.

The word first. Latin *penicillus*, "little tail," which is a diminutive of *peniculus*, "little brush," which is a diminutive of *penis*, which meant tail before it meant anything else. So a pencil is a little little tail. Originally it was a fine brush — the artist's pencil, the thing you'd paint with — and the word only migrated to the graphite stick later. Meanwhile "pen" comes from *penna*, feather, completely unrelated, and the two words just happen to sit next to each other in English looking like siblings.

Fleming in 1928 named his mold *Penicillium* because under the microscope its spore-bearing structures look like tiny brushes. So penicillin and pencil share a root, and the root is tail.

The graphite. Sometime in the 1500s — the usual date is around 1565 but nobody's sure — a storm in Borrowdale, Cumbria, supposedly uprooted a tree and exposed a deposit of pure black stuff. Shepherds used it to mark sheep. It was solid, soft, left a dark line, and wasn't found in that purity anywhere else in the world. They called it *plumbago*, or wad, or black lead, because it looked like lead ore and nobody knew what it actually was. Which is why pencils have "lead" in them, three centuries after everyone knew they didn't. The mineral wasn't named graphite until 1789, when Abraham Gottlob Werner took it from Greek *graphein*, to write — named after the use, which is backward from how minerals usually go.

Borrowdale graphite turned out to be excellent for lining the molds that cast cannonballs — smoother spheres, better ballistics. So the Crown took over the mine, opened it only a few weeks a year, flooded it in between, and made stealing graphite a felony. There was a smuggling trade. Armed guards. Over a rock that shepherds had been scribbling on sheep with.

Then the Napoleonic Wars cut France off from English graphite, and in 1795 Nicolas-Jacques Conté worked out that you could grind up inferior graphite, mix it with clay, and fire it, and by changing the ratio you could control the hardness. That's the H/B scale. Every pencil since is a piece of ceramics. Thoreau's family ran a pencil business in Concord, and Henry David — before the pond — reportedly improved their graphite-clay process enough that Thoreau pencils were considered the best in America for a while.

Why it writes at all. Graphite is carbon arranged in flat hexagonal sheets, and within a sheet the bonds are extremely strong, but between sheets there's almost nothing — just van der Waals attraction. Drag it across paper and the sheets shear off and stay behind. Diamond is the same atoms bonded in every direction instead of in planes, which is why one of them is the hardest natural substance and the other one comes off on your fingers.

If you take sticky tape to a lump of graphite and peel, and then peel the tape against fresh tape, and keep going, you eventually get down to a single sheet of carbon one atom thick. Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov did this in Manchester in 2004, and that's graphene, and they got the Nobel Prize in 2010 for it. Geim had already won an Ig Nobel in 2000 for using a magnetic field to levitate a live frog. He's the only person to hold both.

The eraser. Joseph Priestley, 1770, noticed that a bit of gum from a South American tree was "excellently adapted to the purpose of wiping from paper the marks of a black lead pencil," and the material got its English name from that one job: rubber. Before that people used bread. In 1858 Hymen Lipman patented a pencil with an eraser stuck on the end. The patent was eventually thrown out by the U.S. Supreme Court in 1875 on the grounds that gluing two known things together isn't an invention — the pencil still worked as a pencil, the eraser as an eraser, nothing new emerged. Which is a strange ruling to read now, in the age of the smartphone.

The yellow. Hardtmuth's Koh-i-Noor pencil, shown at the 1889 Paris exposition, was painted yellow — the story is that it was to signal the Siberian graphite inside, and yellow read as Chinese, and Chinese read as fine — and it was named after the diamond. The other carbon. Everyone copied the yellow, so now the default pencil color in a lot of the world is an 1889 marketing decision about the same element in a different crystal.

I want to know what the shepherds called it before anyone else arrived.

Okay. "Still." It caught me when I typed it the first time, so.

Start with the fact that there are two of them, and they're strangers. The *still* that means motionless comes from Old English *stille*, Germanic, back to a root *stel-* meaning to stand, to put in place. It's cousin to *stall* — a standing-place for an animal. The other *still*, the copper thing in a shed, is chopped off the front of *distill*, Latin *destillare*, and that one goes back to *stilla*, a drop. So one *still* is about standing and the other is about falling. And the falling one is the slowest falling there is — a vapor rising, cooling, gathering itself into a drop, letting go, one at a time. If you wanted to design a machine that made motion look like stillness, you'd build a still.

*Stilla* has other children. *Instill* is literally to drip into. *Stillicide* — a real word, a Roman legal term — is the dripping of rainwater off your eaves onto your neighbor's land, and whether you're allowed to. Somewhere there's a two-thousand-year-old dispute about a gutter, filed under a word that sounds like a murder.

Back to the standing one. How does "motionless" become "yet"? *I still love you.* Nothing in that sentence is standing still. The path, as far as I can tell: motionless → unchanging → continuously → even now. Something that doesn't move is something that stays the same, and something that stays the same is something that's still there when you look again. The temporal sense is the spatial sense seen from later. And the concessive one — "Still, it was a good day" — is the same move: despite what was just said, the thing *stands*. It holds its ground. The old meaning is hiding in plain sight in the most throwaway use.

German kept the other fork. *Still* in German mostly means quiet, not motionless — *Stille Nacht* is silent night. And the verb *stillen* means to soothe, to quench, to stanch a wound — and to breastfeed. *Die Stillzeit*, the nursing period. To still a child. English has a trace of this: you can still the waters, still a fear. But we mostly moved *still* toward the eye, and German kept it near the ear. Same word, two senses, two languages each picking one to live in.

*Stillbirth* is the quiet one. The child is still.

The painters. Dutch *stilleven*, 17th century, the first term for the genre — *stil* plus *leven*, a life, a living model, but one that keeps still. A hundred years later French arrives at *nature morte*, dead nature, and it's the same pile of lemons and pewter but you can feel the temperature drop. The Dutch phrase says the objects are patient. The French phrase says they're corpses. English took the Dutch side, which I'm glad about.

Film: a *still*. One frame pulled out of the twenty-four that make a second. The still is what motion is made of, and you can only see it by stopping. Muybridge's horse — the argument about whether all four hooves leave the ground — could only be settled by making the running horse hold still, twelve times, in a row.

Elijah on the mountain, 1 Kings 19. Wind, then earthquake, then fire, and God isn't in any of them, and then *qol demamah daqqah*. The King James gives "a still small voice," which is one of the great phrases in the language. But the Hebrew is stranger — *demamah* is silence, *daqqah* is thin, fine, crushed to powder. "A sound of thin silence." "A voice of sheer silence." A sound that is a silence. The translators had to choose, and they chose *still*, which in 1611 could hold both quiet and motionless at once, and so could carry something the word can barely carry now.

Eliot knew. "At the still point of the turning world." The line only works because *still* is unstable — is the point unmoving, or is it *yet* there, or is it hushed? "Neither arrest nor movement," he says, refusing to let you pick.

Physics, briefly: nothing is still. Relativity took away absolute rest. Quantum mechanics took away the rest of it — even at absolute zero there's zero-point motion, which is why helium won't freeze at ordinary pressure no matter how cold you make it. The atoms can't stop. So the standing-*still* names something that doesn't exist, and the yet-*still* names the only thing that does — persistence, the thing being there when you look again.

I keep coming back to the still in the shed. Drop, drop. Each one a small letting-go. The whole apparatus doing nothing, visibly, for hours, and at the end there's something clear in the flask that wasn't there before.
